title: Fibre by Fibre
series: Fibre by Fibre, an illustrated essay on paper
style: a quiet page of washi: off-white paper with visible fibres, sumi-ink brush lines that bleed slightly, Barlow type, a single vermilion seal
context: The video explains paper, following the Fibre by Fibre essay. Paper is a mat of plant cellulose fibres, mostly air, bonded by hydrogen bonds as water leaves. Fibre lengths (average): kozo ~10 mm (6–20), used for washi, hanji; hardwood eucalyptus ~0.9 mm, copy paper; widths 10–40 µm. Hand papermaking (washi): harvest, steam and strip bark, clean, beat, mix with water and neri (formation aid), dip and sway the mould (su), couch, press, dry on boards. History: traditional date Cai Lun 105 CE; fragments from the 1st century BCE, contested Fangmatan map possibly older; Korea and Japan within centuries; Dunhuang; Talas 751 story deemed unlikely by Jonathan Bloom; Baghdad by 794; Cairo, Fez; Xàtiva, Spain by 1056; Fabriano: gelatin sizing and the first watermarks 1282; Nuremberg 1390; Mexico City 1575; Germantown 1690; amate bark paper ~75 BCE (not strictly paper). Washi households: ~70,000 in 1901, under 500 by 1984, 295 in 2009. World production ~401 million tonnes a year, more than double 1980; packaging up, printing papers lowest since 1987. Laid lines 7–10 per cm, chain lines 22–32 mm apart; raking light reveals relief. Hot-pressed, cold-pressed (NOT), rough watercolour papers. Ink wicking follows Lucas–Washburn (distance ∝ √time); sizing raises the contact angle; raw xuan is unsized. Rendering paper: Perlin gradient noise (2002 quintic), fractal Brownian motion (feTurbulence), formation, fibres (Guo & Kunii 1991), normals from a height field, Lambert lighting.
